summary: Economists expect the Bank of Canada to raise rates on Wednesday, Ottawa and Washington trade jabs over tariffs and 'interference', and Toronto votes Monday.
body: Most economists in a Reuters poll expect the Bank of Canada to raise its key interest rate on Wednesday, Oct. 28, from 2.25% to 2.50%, its first move in a year [^1]. A large minority, 15 of 34, expect no change because the economy is weak [^1]. The worry is prices: inflation was 3.1% in September, just above the Bank's 1% to 3% target range, driven by gasoline, which was up 27.8% from a year earlier [^2]. A hike would make borrowing, such as mortgages and car loans, more expensive. For students, Statistics Canada also reports that Ontario tuition fees rose 2.1% this year, the biggest jump since 2018, after the province ended its tuition freeze [^2].

With Canada, the White House will drop tariffs on some Canadian goods, including plywood, some paper products and some machinery, and add them on certain valves and carpets, from the end of October; analysts say the change mostly helps U.S. Senator Susan Collins of Maine [^3]. Trump says a deal is close and that the U.S. has "all the cards" [^3]. Separately, the U.S. embassy accused Canadian ministers and premiers of trying to influence U.S. politics. Prime Minister Mark Carney said "there is no merit to these claims" [^4]. In Hamilton, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly gave Stelco's U.S. owner, Cleveland-Cliffs, 15 days to keep its promise to protect jobs or face legal action; the company says the layoffs are temporary and caused by tariffs [^5].

Toronto and other Ontario cities vote on Monday, Oct. 26. In the last mayoral debate, Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford clashed over housing, a property tax freeze and a plan to turn Toronto Water into an independent utility [^6]. Polls released this week showed a close race, with results depending on the pollster [^7].
differences: On rates, most economists polled expect a hike, but 15 of 34 expect none [^1]. The U.S. embassy says Canadian leaders are meddling in U.S. politics; Carney says the claims have no merit [^4]. Ottawa says Cleveland-Cliffs broke its job promise; the company says it will fight in court [^5].
